passage:
"Vijay, why is the sink full again? I asked you..."
Ritu stopped mid-sentence.
"What?" Vijay asked, wary.
"Give me a minute." She closed her eyes. Jaw: clenched. Shoulders: up by her ears. Stomach: hollow. Breath: short.
"I haven't eaten since eleven," she said slowly. "And I've been hunched over spreadsheets all day."
"So... you're not angry about the sink?"
"A bit. But mostly I'm starving and tired."
Vijay laughed with relief. "There's dal. I'll heat it."
She ate standing at the counter, rolling her shoulders. Ten minutes later she said, "Okay. About the sink. Can we take turns?"
"Sounds fair," Vijay said. "And good catch."

qa.q: Since when had Ritu not eaten?
What did Ritu discover she was really feeling during her pause?
qa.a: She realised she was mostly starving and tired, with a clenched jaw and tight shoulders, not mainly angry about the sink.
Pausing to check her jaw, shoulders, stomach and breath, because it showed hunger and fatigue before she snapped.

qa.q: How did Vijay feel when Ritu stopped mid-sentence?
qa.a: Vijay was wary at first, then relieved when she said she was mostly hungry and tired.

grounding: It shows a person pausing to check jaw, shoulders, stomach and breathing, discovering hunger and fatigue before they turn into snapping.

passage:
I learned the body scan from Vijay, the oldest cashier at our bank branch. He does it every day at four. I used to think it was a bit silly.
Then last March I nearly shouted at a customer who asked the same question twice. I went to the staff room shaking. I thought I was just angry at him.
So I tried Vijay's minute. Jaw first: clenched hard. Shoulders: stiff. Stomach: knotted. Breathing: fast and shallow. I realised I was completely worn out. I'd skipped lunch and worked late all week.
Now I do it at four too. Some days it tells me to eat. Some days to walk to the water cooler. Once it told me to take a real day off, and I did.
I haven't snapped at anyone since.

Sarika

qa.q: At what time does Vijay do the body scan?
qa.a: He does it every day at four.

qa.q: What did Sarika realise during the first body scan?
qa.a: Sarika found a clenched jaw, stiff shoulders, a knotted stomach and fast breathing, and realised the real feeling was exhaustion, not just anger.

qa.q: Why is the four o'clock check-in a good habit for Sarika?
qa.a: It catches hunger, tiredness or stress early, so Sarika can eat, walk or rest before snapping or burning out.

qa.q: How might the customer have felt if Sarika had shouted?
qa.a: The customer might have felt hurt or confused, since asking the same question twice isn't a big thing.

grounding: It shows a person using a one-minute body check-in to notice stress, hunger and fatigue before they turn into snapping or burnout.
